title: Work
description: Jobs and the office: say what you do and where you work, use mir, dir and ihm with helfen, and give reasons with weil. Then a first day at a new job.

grammarNotes.title: Jobs: no article, and -in for women
grammarNotes.body:
To say what someone does, use **sein** and the job with **no article**. English says *a teacher*, German doesn't:

- *Ich bin **Lehrerin**.* = I'm a teacher.
- *Er ist **Koch**.* = He's a cook.

To ask: **Was sind Sie von Beruf?** or, to a friend, **Was bist du von Beruf?** (literally *What are you by profession?*)

Add **-in** for a woman, like *Freund → Freundin*. Some jobs add an umlaut too: *Arzt → Ärztin, Koch → Köchin*. The plural of *-in* is always **-innen**: *zwei Lehrerinnen*.

Watch out: **der Chef** is the boss, never a cook. A cook is **der Koch**.

grammarNotes.title: Where you work: im, bei and als
grammarNotes.body:
Three little words answer **Wo arbeitest du?**

- **in** for the place you sit: *im Büro, in einem Restaurant*. It takes the dative, as in Unit 12.
- **bei** for the company or organisation: *bei einer Firma, bei der Post*. Treat it just like *mit*: it always takes the dative, so *die* becomes *der* and *eine* becomes *einer*.
- **als** for the job you do, with no article: *als Kellner*.

*Ich bin Kellner* and *Ich arbeite als Kellner* mean the same thing.
table: Sie arbeitet bei einer Firma in Hamburg.

grammarNotes.title: mir, dir, ihm: the dative pronouns
grammarNotes.body:
Just as *der* becomes *dem* after *mit*, the words for *I, you, he* … have a **dative** form. You already know some of them from fixed phrases: *Wie geht es **dir**? Das gefällt **mir**. Was fehlt **Ihnen**?*

Use them:

- after **mit, zu** and **bei**: *Kommst du mit **mir**?*
- with **helfen**: *Ich helfe **dir**.*

**ihr** now has three jobs: *ihr* (you all), *ihr* (her, as in *ihr Bruder*) and *ihr* (to her). The sentence tells you which.

Don't mix these up with **mich** and **dich**, as in *Freut mich!* That's a different form, which you'll meet later.
table: Das Kind ist krank. Wie geht es ihm?

grammarNotes.title: helfen: help someone with the dative
grammarNotes.body:
**helfen** changes **e → i** in the *du* and *er / sie / es* forms, like *nehmen* and *sprechen*.

The person you help always takes the **dative**: *Ich helfe **dir**. Der Chef hilft **ihm**.* English says *help him*, so this feels odd at first.

Add **gern** to sound friendly: *Ich helfe dir gern!* = I'm happy to help you!

grammarNotes.title: weil: the verb goes to the end
grammarNotes.body:
**weil** = because. It joins a reason onto a sentence, and it changes the word order: in the *weil* part, the verb with the ending goes to the **very end**.

- Put a **comma** before *weil*.
- With a modal verb, the modal goes last, after the other verb: *weil ich arbeiten **muss***.
- *war* and *hatte* go last too: *weil ich krank **war***.

To answer **Warum?** (why?), you can use the *weil* part on its own: *Warum lernst du Deutsch? **Weil ich in Berlin arbeite.***

You may also hear **denn** (because). After *denn* the verb stays second: *Ich bin müde, denn ich arbeite viel.* In everyday speech, *weil* is much more common.

exercises.title: Was sind Sie von Beruf?
exercises.body:
**der Beruf** = the job, the profession.

To ask what someone does:

- **Was sind Sie von Beruf?** (polite)
- **Was bist du von Beruf?** (a friend)

Literally *What are you by profession?* Answer with **sein** and the job, with **no article**: *Ich bin Lehrer.* English says *a teacher*, German doesn't.

examples.translation: What do you do for a living?

exercises.title: Lehrer, Lehrerin
exercises.body:
Most jobs have a form for men and a form for women. Add **-in** for a woman, just like *Freund → Freundin*:

- der Lehrer → die **Lehrerin** (teacher)
- der Kellner → die **Kellnerin** (waiter, waitress)
- der Verkäufer → die **Verkäuferin** (shop assistant), from Unit 11

Some add an umlaut too. You know *Arzt → Ärztin* from Unit 8. **der Koch** (cook) works the same way: die **Köchin**.

examples.hint: Koch has the back-of-throat ch; Köchin has the soft one

exercises.translation: My mother is a cook.
exercises.hint: der Koch → the female form (with an umlaut)

exercises.title: No article with jobs
exercises.body:
After **sein**, a job has no *ein* or *eine*:

- *Ich bin Lehrerin.* ✔
- *Ich bin eine Lehrerin.* ✘

But when you talk about a **person**, not their job, the article comes back as usual: ***Der** Kellner spricht Englisch.* = The waiter speaks English.

examples.text: Er ist Koch in einem Restaurant.
examples.translation: He's a cook in a restaurant.

exercises.translation: What do you do for a living? (formal)

exercises.title: Plurals: -innen
exercises.body:
The plural of every *-in* word ends in **-innen**:

- die Lehrerin → zwei **Lehrerinnen**
- die Köchin → zwei **Köchinnen**

The men's forms ending in *-er* don't change: *ein Lehrer, zwei Lehrer*. And **der Koch** becomes **die Köche**.

accepted: My brother is a shop assistant.
My brother is a sales assistant.
My brother is a sales clerk.

exercises.title: im Büro, bei einer Firma
exercises.body:
You know **Wo arbeitest du?** Here are two ways to answer:

- **das Büro** = the office. Where you sit is *in* + dative, as in Unit 12: **im Büro**.
- **die Firma** = the company. For the company you work for, use **bei**: *Ich arbeite **bei einer Firma**.*

**bei** is new, but treat it just like *mit*: it always takes the dative. So *die Firma* → **bei der Firma**, *eine Firma* → **bei einer Firma**.

examples.text: Sie arbeitet bei einer Firma in Hamburg.

exercises.title: als Kellner: as a waiter
exercises.body:
To say what job you do, use **als** (as) + the job. Just like after *sein*, there's **no article**:

- *Ich arbeite **als** Kellner.* = I work as a waiter.
- *Ich bin Kellner.* = I'm a waiter.

Both mean the same. You can add the place too: *Sie arbeitet als Köchin in einem Restaurant.*

examples.text: Sie arbeitet als Köchin in einem Restaurant.
examples.translation: She works as a cook in a restaurant.

examples.text: Er arbeitet als Lehrer in Wien.

exercises.title: Kollegen und Chefs
exercises.body:
The people you work with:

- **der Kollege** / **die Kollegin** = the colleague
- **der Chef** / **die Chefin** = the boss

Careful: **der Chef** is the boss, not a cook! A cook is *der Koch*.

Plurals: *die Kollegen, die Kolleginnen, die Chefs, die Chefinnen*.

exercises.title: You already know mir and dir
exercises.body:
Look at some phrases you already know:

- *Wie geht es **dir**?* (literally *How goes it for you?*)
- *Das gefällt **mir**.* (literally *That pleases me.*)
- *Was fehlt **Ihnen**?* (literally *What is missing for you?*)

**mir, dir** and **Ihnen** are the **dative** forms of *ich, du* and *Sie*. Just as *der* becomes *dem* after *mit*, these little words change too. In Unit 13 you heard *Mir tut der Kopf weh*. Now you know why!

exercises.title: helfen: to help
exercises.body:
**helfen** = to help. It changes **e → i** in the *du* and *er / sie* forms, like *nehmen*:

- ich helfe
- du **hilfst**
- er / sie **hilft**
- wir helfen
- ihr helft
- sie / Sie helfen

The person you help takes the **dative**: *Kannst du **mir** helfen?* In a question with *können*, *helfen* goes to the end.

exercises.translation: Can you help me?

exercises.instruction: Which form of helfen fits? Die Chefin ___ mir.

exercises.title: ihm and ihr: him and her
exercises.body:
- **er** → **ihm** (him)
- **sie** (she) → **ihr** (her)
- **es** → **ihm**, like *er*

*ihr* has a lot of jobs now: *ihr* (you all), *ihr Bruder* (her brother) and *ich helfe ihr* (I help her). The sentence tells you which one it is.

exercises.before: Anna hat viel Arbeit. Ich helfe
exercises.translation: Anna has a lot of work. I'm helping her.

exercises.title: uns, euch, Ihnen
exercises.body:
- **wir** → **uns** (us)
- **ihr** (you all) → **euch**
- **sie** (they) → **ihnen**
- **Sie** (formal) → **Ihnen**, always with a capital *I*

In a shop you'll often hear **Kann ich Ihnen helfen?** = Can I help you?

exercises.instruction: You work in a shop. A customer comes in. What do you say?

exercises.title: mit mir, mit dir
exercises.body:
After **mit**, **zu** and **bei**, use the dative forms too, just like *mit dem Bus*:

- *mit **mir*** = with me
- *mit **dir*** = with you
- *bei **uns*** = at our place

exercises.title: weil: the verb goes to the end
exercises.body:
**weil** = because. It joins a reason onto a sentence:

- *Ich bin müde. Ich arbeite viel.*
- *Ich bin müde, **weil** ich viel **arbeite**.*

In the *weil* part, the verb with the ending jumps to the **very end**. This is new: until now the verb was always second. Always put a **comma** before *weil*.

**viel** = a lot.

examples.text: Ich bin müde, weil ich viel arbeite.
examples.translation: I'm tired because I work a lot.

examples.text: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Berlin wohne.
examples.translation: I'm learning German because I live in Berlin.

examples.text: Er ist zu Hause, weil er krank ist.
examples.translation: He's at home because he's ill.

exercises.title: Warum? Weil …
exercises.body:
**warum** = why. To answer, you can say just the *weil* part on its own, with the verb at the end:

- *Warum lernst du Deutsch?*
- ***Weil** ich in Berlin **arbeite**.*

In the question, *warum* works like *wo* or *was*: the verb comes second.

exercises.before: Warum lernst du Deutsch? Weil ich in Berlin
exercises.translation: Why are you learning German? Because I work in Berlin.
exercises.hint: arbeiten → ich …, at the very end

exercises.title: weil ich arbeiten muss
exercises.body:
With a modal verb, the **modal goes last**, after the other verb:

- *Ich muss arbeiten.*
- *Ich komme nicht, weil ich arbeiten **muss**.*

*war* and *hatte* also go to the end:

- *Ich war nicht da, weil ich krank **war**.*
- *Ich bin nicht gekommen, weil ich keine Zeit **hatte**.*

examples.text: Ich komme nicht, weil ich arbeiten muss.
examples.translation: I'm not coming because I have to work.

examples.text: Er lernt Deutsch, weil er in Wien wohnen will.
examples.translation: He's learning German because he wants to live in Vienna.

examples.text: Ich war nicht da, weil ich krank war.
examples.translation: I wasn't there because I was ill.

exercises.translation: I wasn't there because I was ill.

exercises.title: Geld verdienen
exercises.body:
- **verdienen** = to earn
- **das Geld** = money

Like *be-* verbs, verbs starting with **ver-** take no *ge-* in the Perfekt: *Ich habe gut **verdient**.*

**Wie viel** = how much. But careful: in Germany, *Wie viel verdienst du?* is a very personal question!

examples.text: Ich arbeite am Samstag, weil ich Geld verdienen muss.
examples.translation: I work on Saturdays because I have to earn money.

exercises.before: Sie arbeitet viel, weil sie Geld verdienen
exercises.translation: She works a lot because she has to earn money.
exercises.hint: müssen → sie …, at the very end

exercises.title: Besprechung and E-Mail
exercises.body:
Two words for office life:

- **die Besprechung** = the meeting (at work)
- **die E-Mail** = the email. In Germany it's *die*.

You can use them in a *weil* part too: *Ich kann nicht kommen, weil ich eine Besprechung **habe**.*

exercises.title: Working hours
exercises.body:
Two more words for the working day:

- **der Feierabend** = the end of the working day, and the free time after it (literally *party evening*). **Ich habe um fünf Uhr Feierabend.** = I finish work at five.
- **die Pause** = the break. **Pause machen** = to take a break.

And for working hours: **von** neun **bis** fünf = from nine to five.

examples.translation: I finish work at five o'clock.
When are we taking a break?

examples.text: Wir arbeiten von neun bis fünf.
examples.translation: We work from nine to five.

exercises.title: Neu im Büro
exercises.body: It's Emma's first day at a new job. Her colleague Jonas shows her around. Colleagues often say *du* to each other in Germany. Read along, and tap each line to hear it.

examples.text: Hallo! Bist du neu hier? Ich bin Jonas.
examples.translation: Jonas: Hi! Are you new here? I'm Jonas.

examples.text: Ja, ich heiße Emma. Freut mich!
examples.translation: Emma: Yes, my name's Emma. Nice to meet you!

examples.text: Freut mich auch! Komm, das ist dein Büro. Und da links ist die Küche. Wo hast du letztes Jahr gearbeitet?
examples.translation: Jonas: Nice to meet you too! Come on, this is your office. And there on the left is the kitchen. Where did you work last year?

examples.text: Ich war Verkäuferin, aber ich habe nicht viel verdient. Und du?

examples.text: Ich arbeite hier im Büro. Aber letztes Jahr war ich Koch in einem Restaurant!

examples.text: Koch? Warum arbeitest du jetzt im Büro?
examples.translation: Emma: A cook? Why do you work in an office now?

examples.text: Weil ich am Wochenende nicht arbeiten will. Hier arbeiten wir von neun bis fünf. Um fünf Uhr habe ich Feierabend!
examples.translation: Jonas: Because I don't want to work at weekends. Here we work from nine to five. At five o'clock I finish work!

examples.text: Super! Und wer ist die Chefin?
examples.translation: Emma: Great! And who's the boss?

examples.text: Frau Schulz. Sie ist toll und hilft dir gern. Um zehn Uhr haben wir eine Besprechung. Du kannst mit mir gehen.
examples.translation: Jonas: Ms Schulz. She's great and she's happy to help you. At ten o'clock we have a meeting. You can go with me.

examples.text: Danke! Und wann machen wir Pause?

examples.text: Um zwölf Uhr. Dann essen wir zusammen in der Küche, okay?

Emma: Yes, I'd love to! Thanks, Jonas!
